The World Today · ABC listen

Question mark hangs over warming of US-Chinese relations

Broadcast Friday, 19 October 2001 · Reporter: Michael Vincent

← Full The World Today episode — Friday, 19 October 2001

ELEANOR HALL: Well, despite the anthrax fears at home, President George W. Bush is on his first official visit to China for the APEC Summit in Shanghai. The visit by the US President marks a significant shift in the relationship between the two major powers.

Just six months ago the United States and China were sparring over the downed American spy plane and increased US arm sales to Taiwan. But in the wake of the September 11 attacks and China's support for the US campaign against terrorism, relations have warmed considerably.

However, as Michael Vincent reports, some analysts are asking what price the United States is paying for this new Chinese friendship.

MICHAEL VINCENT: In April this year, President George Bush, fresh into his new job, found himself asking China to return the crew of one of his spy planes.

GEORGE W. BUSH: This accident has the potential of undermining our hopes for a fruitful and productive relationship between our two countries. To keep that from happening, our service men and women need to come home.

MICHAEL VINCENT: Now it seems the relationship of the two world powers has gone full circle. Colombia University China specialist, Professor Andrew Nathan.

PROFESSOR ANDREW NATHAN: At the time of the spy plane incident that Bush people didn't trust the Chinese government and the Chinese government was afraid that the Bush people would get off on an anti-China tilt. Now that concern is behind US, the Bush people have decided that they do trust the Chinese government and have to. And so the Chinese government can relax and can begin to work with the Bush people.

MICHAEL VINCENT: So as President Bush looks to strengthen his international coalition against terrorism in Shanghai, issues such as Taiwan and human rights abuses are expected to be off his agenda, much to the relief of the Chinese.

Also playing into the hands of the Chinese, the campaign against terrorism, which the Director of International Studies at the University of Technology, Sydney, Professor David Goodman, says has seen Chinese pursue Muslim dissidents in their western provinces.

PROFESSOR DAVID GOODMAN: The Chinese government has used the opportunity of American action in Afghanistan to launch an even more increased suppression of separatist activities in Chiang Jaing [phonetic], which is the Chinese province that borders on Central Asia, or one of them.

MICHAEL VINCENT: Those actions against dissidents in China, how long do you think the US will continue to turn a blind eye to them?

PROFESSOR DAVID GOODMAN: Oh, I think as long as the current situation pertains. That's to say as long as the United States is involved in a war in Afghanistan and requires the support of surrounding countries and the understanding of the surrounding countries, these situations are going to continue.

MICHAEL VINCENT: Meanwhile, Taiwan is anxiously watching for signals from President Bush as to whether he will continue to support armed sales to them. At APEC, China has opposed a political representative from Taipei from attending. APEC is a grouping of economies, so China has allowed the attendance of a Taiwanese economist.

Professor Nathan believes the relationship between the US and China may be complicated by the fact that he believes Taipei may indeed be looking for a thaw in its own relations with Beijing.

PROFESSOR ANDREW NATHAN: They haven't really entered a thaw, but I see a lot of signs that both sides are willing to try again on the track of talks and negotiations. So that if that's Taiwan's strategy anyhow then they really don't lose that much.

ELEANOR HALL: China's specialist at Colombia University, Professor Andrew Nathan speaking to Michael Vincent.
